sources.note: Optimality of the forking-lemma loss for algebraic reductions under OMDL. EUROCRYPT 2012, LNCS 7237, pp. 554-571, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-29011-4_33. Verified in vendor/cryptobib: cryptobib_key EC:Seurin12.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction (Fiat-Shamir applied to Schnorr identification) using only the group operation; the Pointcheval-Stern reduction runs any EUF-CMA forger only as an oracle — it simulates signing with the HVZK simulator and random-oracle programming, then reruns the forger on the same coins with a reprogrammed oracle (forking). pages.statement: If [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] is hard, EUF-CMA-secure [[digital-signature|digital signatures]] exist in the [[random-oracle-model|random-oracle model]]: Schnorr signatures — the [[fiat-shamir-heuristic|Fiat-Shamir transform]] [[FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems|FS86]] applied to the Schnorr identification protocol [[Sch91 - Efficient signature generation by smart cards|Sch91]] — are EUF-CMA secure under DLOG in the ROM — [[PS96 - Security Proofs for Signature Schemes|PS96]].
pages.sketch: The reduction answers signing queries with simulated transcripts (sample $z, e$ uniformly, set $a = g^z h^{-e}$, program the random oracle to $e$ at $(a, m)$) and forks the forger: it reruns the forger on the same coins with the oracle reprogrammed at the forgery's query. Two forgeries $(a, e, z)$, $(a, e', z')$ with $e \neq e'$ give $x = (z - z')/(e - e')$, the discrete logarithm of $h$.

sources.ref_file_title: BCMS20 - Recursive Proof Composition from Accumulation Schemes
sources.authors: Benedikt Bünz, Alessandro Chiesa, Pratyush Mishra, Nicholas Spooner
sources.note: Explicit polynomial-commitment abstraction PC_DL of the Pedersen-plus-IPA scheme with a security proof under DLOG in the ROM. TCC 2020, LNCS 12551, pp. 1-18, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-64378-2_1. The eprint version (2020/499) is titled 'Proof-Carrying Data from Accumulation Schemes'; the file uses the proceedings title. Verified in vendor/cryptobib: cryptobib_key TCC:BCMS20.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction (Pedersen vector commitment plus the recursive inner-product argument) built from the group operation, and a security reduction that uses the adversary only as an oracle: the extractor rewinds the prover over a tree of challenges (special-soundness tree extraction; forking in the non-interactive ROM version), and two openings of one Pedersen commitment to distinct polynomials yield a discrete-log relation among the public generators. No dependence on adversary code.
pages.model_justification: The wiki's PCS syntax is non-interactive ($\Open$ outputs a proof $\pi$). The DLOG-based scheme obtains non-interactive openings by applying Fiat-Shamir to the public-coin inner-product argument, and its security is proven under DLOG in the ROM (BCMS20). The underlying interactive public-coin protocol of BCCGP16 is standard-model.
pages.statement: If [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] is hard in a prime-order group, a transparent [[polynomial-commitment|polynomial commitment scheme]] exists: commit to the coefficient vector with a Pedersen vector commitment and prove $f(z) = y$ with the recursive inner-product argument, giving $O(\log d)$-size openings, $O(d)$ verifier time, and no trusted setup — [[BCCGP16 - Efficient Zero-Knowledge Arguments for Arithmetic Circuits in the Discrete Log Setting|BCCGP16]]. The non-interactive scheme applies Fiat-Shamir to the public-coin protocol and is proven secure under DLOG in the ROM — [[BCMS20 - Recursive Proof Composition from Accumulation Schemes|BCMS20]].
pages.sketch: The claim $f(z) = y$ is the inner product $\langle \vec{f}, (1, z, \dots, z^d) \rangle = y$. Each round folds both vectors in half with a random challenge; after $\log d$ rounds the prover reveals the two remaining scalars and the verifier checks one commitment equation. The extractor rewinds each round to build a tree of accepting transcripts, and two openings of one commitment to distinct polynomials give a nontrivial discrete-log relation among the public generators.

sources.ref_file_title: BM84 - How to Generate Cryptographically Strong Sequences of Pseudo-Random Bits

sources.note: Next-bit test characterization of pseudorandomness; PRGs from any one-way permutation. FOCS 1982, pp. 80-91. pages.class_justification: One fixed construction (iterated exponentiation with the half-interval predicate) using only the group operation; the reduction turns any distinguisher into a next-bit predictor by a hybrid argument and the predictor into a DLOG solver by BM84's square-root recovery, calling the adversary only as an oracle.
pages.statement: If [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] is hard in $\ZZ_p^*$, the Blum-Micali generator is a [[pseudorandom-generator|PRG]]: from a uniform seed $x_0$, iterate $x_{i+1} = g^{x_i} \bmod p$ and output at each step the bit $[x_i \ge (p-1)/2]$, the most significant bit of the discrete logarithm of $x_{i+1}$ — [[BM84 - How to Generate Cryptographically Strong Sequences of Pseudo-Random Bits|BM84]].
pages.sketch: The half-interval predicate is hard-core for $x \mapsto g^x$: Euler's criterion gives the parity of $x$, and the predicate identifies which square root of $y g^{-(x \bmod 2)}$ has index $\lfloor x/2 \rfloor$, so recursing recovers $x$ bit by bit; a predictor with only noticeable advantage is first amplified by random self-reduction. A distinguisher for the generator yields such a predictor by the next-bit test — [[Yao82a - Theory and Applications of Trapdoor Functions|Yao82a]].

sources.ref_file_title: BP02 - GQ and Schnorr Identification Schemes Proofs of Security against Impersonation under Active and Concurrent Attacks
sources.note: Active and concurrent impersonation security under the one-more discrete logarithm assumption; Reset Lemma. CRYPTO 2002, LNCS 2442, pp. 162-177. Verified in vendor/cryptobib: cryptobib_key C:BelPal02.

pages.class_justification: Fixed protocol built from the group operation; the security reduction runs any passive impersonator as an oracle, rewinding it to two accepting transcripts with the same commitment and distinct challenges, from which special soundness computes the discrete logarithm. No dependence on the impersonator's code.
pages.model_justification: The identification protocol and its passive-impersonation security proof use no random oracle; model rom on this page is a leftover from the signature edge. The ROM enters only in the separate Fiat-Shamir edge to Schnorr signatures.
pages.statement: The [[digital-signature#schnorr-signatures|Schnorr identification protocol]] is a three-move sigma protocol for knowledge of $x = \log_g h$: the prover sends $a = g^r$, receives a random challenge $e$, and replies $z = r + ex$; the verifier accepts iff $g^z = a h^e$. It is special sound and perfectly honest-verifier zero-knowledge unconditionally, and secure against impersonation under passive attack if [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] is hard — [[Sch91 - Efficient signature generation by smart cards|Sch91]].
pages.sketch: Rewinding an impersonator to two accepting transcripts $(a, e, z)$, $(a, e', z')$ with $e \neq e'$ yields $x = (z - z')/(e - e')$; eavesdropped transcripts are simulated by sampling $z, e$ uniformly and setting $a = g^z h^{-e}$, which reproduces the honest distribution exactly.
pages.security_loss: Reset Lemma: a passive impersonator with success $\varepsilon$ yields a DLOG solver with success at least $(\varepsilon - 1/|C|)^2$, $C$ the challenge space — BP02.
pages.improvements_text: - Security against impersonation under active and concurrent attacks, under the one-more discrete logarithm assumption — [[BP02 - GQ and Schnorr Identification Schemes Proofs of Security against Impersonation under Active and Concurrent Attacks|BP02]]
